body: I don't think these should be public yet while they're work-in-progress.

I'm guessing this lazy construction is modeled after `get_gdtype_static_mutable`?

I think the design of Godot's typing startup sequence isn't in a great state. `GDType` are only lazily created for `Object` because they have to (backwards compat to the current state of the code). 
Have you tried implementing this without lazy evaluation and seeing if anything breaks?

I'm not a huge fan of silent error recovery.
Let's add an error message, unless you tested this and found it triggers too often in normal usage?
Needs a comment to signify that this is connected to the GDType values.
Why check on `variant_constants`? This wasn't the case before, was it?
Why all the changes to this function? Shouldn't `variant_values` be largely unaffected?
Why check on `variant_constants`, this wasn't the case before?

This is likely quite a lot slower than the previous implementation.
Any reason not to iterate `get_integer_constant_map(false)` and count the number of values in each enum?
I'm not sure I understand what you're doing here, shouldn't this just be `get_gdtype(p_type).get_integer_constant_map(false).has(p_value) `?
So private or protected?
The lowest accessibility that is possible to achieve right now. Remove if nothing needs it.
Yes, it is. I don't think anything would break in this case since they all get initialized at engine startup. Will change.
It should ideally never trigger, so I'll toss in an error macro.

So, before, the three different methods (`add_constant`, `add_enum_constant`, and `add_variant_constant`) all had different levels of checking for each other; I simply unified them so that they all check for each other. 
They should never (and currently indeed never do) have members with the same. This just hardcodes that check. 

It is technically unnecessary and maybe outside the scope of this PR, but since I was touching that code, I deemed it only fit to bring it up to what I consider a reasonable standard. 

Think of it this way, if those checks aren't hardcoded, a type could have a variant constant and an int constant (or enum) with the same name... Yeah no.

`add_enum_constant` was using the following code:
```
enum_data[p_type].value[p_enum_type_name][p_enumeration_name] = p_enum_value;
enum_data[p_type].value_to_enum[p_enumeration_name] = p_enum_type_name;
```
This means it was not adding it to either `constant_data[p_type]` (it was using the `EnumData` struct, not the `ConstantData` struct). So the number of values in each enum were not counted. `Variant` did not include enum values in integer constants.

This approach should result in the same number as before, namely integer constants + variant constants. 
I could be wrong though, and please do let me know if so.

Same as for `get_constants_count_for_type`, afaik `Variant` was not treating enums as constants. I don't know why, but that's how it was (unless I misunderstood the code).

I actually believe they should be counted, it's just that it would be a change from the existing model, so I didn't do it. This is especially relevant for `has_constant()` which will return false for enum values even though they are exposed all the same... Same logic for me as with the newly added checks for adding new integer/enum/variant constants cross-checking each other.

Looking at when the existing checks were added, it looks like they were just added here when bugfixing other things, and weren't as thorough as they should have been https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/99424 https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/38891

Just saw the edit, was typing out my comment whilst that happened, I guess. As far as speed, there's really not much that can be done about it? The fact that `GDType` does not support non-enum integer constants to be directly accessed kind of prevents it from being made faster than through the loop for that part. 

Now, just like the counting thing, this is all because `Variant` does not consider enums as constants (not even talking about enum values, just the enums themselves). Why? I'm not sure. 
* If we depart from this model, which I would be in favor of, then the counting would become as fast as it used to be again. 

This method is only there for GDNative, added by #44733 , with the intent of pre-allocating buffers with the correct size. I don't think that we need to worry too much about performance, as it's a one-off operation.

It could be made faster by counting instead of using a `List`. But I just looked and `get_constants_count_for_type` seems to be completely unused. So there's no reason why we should spend time making it fast (if anything it could be dropped, but keeping it with your implementation is fine too).
